hand down: pass something, such as clothes or traditions, to younger people
typical: hand sth down (to sb), from parent to child. NOT for: giving something to a person right now.
This ring was handed down from my grandmother.
She hands her old clothes down to her younger sister.
officially announce a decision or punishment
typical: hand down a verdict/sentence/ruling (court). NOT for: telling friends news.
The judge handed down a five-year sentence.
The court will hand down its decision on Monday.
hand in: give something such as work or a form to a teacher, boss or official
typical: hand in homework, hand sth in. NOT for: giving something to a friend (use hand or give).
Please hand in your essays by Friday.
I handed the form in at the front desk.
take something you found to the police or an office
typical: hand in a wallet/a lost phone. NOT for: arresting someone.
She found a wallet and handed it in at the police station.
Someone handed in a lost phone this morning.
formally say you are leaving your job
typical: hand in your notice/resignation. NOT for: being fired.
He handed in his notice last week.
She decided to hand in her resignation after the meeting.
hand out: give something to each person in a group
typical: hand out leaflets/papers, hand sth out. NOT for: giving something to only one person.
The teacher handed out the exam papers.
Volunteers were handing leaflets out at the station.
give advice, a punishment or praise
typical: hand out advice/a fine/a ban. NOT for: receiving something.
The referee handed out three yellow cards.
He loves to hand out advice nobody asked for.
hand over: typical: hand sth over (to sb), hand over the keys/money. NOT for: leaving something for later.
Please hand over your passport at the desk.
He handed the keys over without a word.
give power or control to someone else
typical: hand over control/power/responsibility (to sb). NOT for: sharing it.
The old director handed over the company to his daughter.
Power will be handed over to the new government in May.
pass a phone call or a broadcast to someone else
typical: I'll hand you over to sb. NOT for: ending a call.
I'll hand you over to my colleague, who knows more.
And now we hand over to Anna for the weather.
hang around: spend time somewhere doing nothing in particular
typical: informal, hang around (a place). NOT for: working hard.
Teenagers often hang around the shopping centre.
We hung around outside until the shop opened.
wait somewhere, often longer than you expected
typical: hang around (for sb/sth). NOT for: leaving quickly.
I can't hang around; my bus leaves in five minutes.
He hung around for an hour waiting for her.
spend time with a person or a group
typical: hang around with sb, informal. NOT for: a close family relationship.
She hangs around with a group of older students.
I used to hang around with them in high school.
hang back: stay behind or not move forward with others
typical: hang back at the door/from the crowd. NOT for: leading the group.
The shy girl hung back at the party door.
Most people hung back while the dog barked.
hesitate to do something because you are not sure
typical: hang back from doing sth. NOT for: acting quickly.
He hung back from asking for a raise.
Don't hang back; say what you think.
hang in: keep trying in a difficult situation
typical: informal, mostly 'hang in there', said to encourage someone. NOT for: staying at a place.
Hang in there, the exams are almost over.
She told him to hang in there and not to give up.
hang on: verb
wait for a short time
typical: informal, hang on a minute/second; spoken. NOT for: waiting a long time.
Hang on a second, I'll get my coat.
Hang on, I think I left my keys in the car.
verb
hold something tightly
typical: hang on (to) sth, hang on tight. NOT for: letting go.
Hang on tight, the road is bumpy.
He hung on with both hands.
verb
continue in a difficult situation and not give up
typical: hang on until help comes. NOT for: stopping.
The climbers hung on until help arrived.
If we can hang on for another week, the project will be finished.
verb
say this when you suddenly notice something strange or remember something, informal
typical: spoken, Hang on! That's not right. NOT for: asking someone to wait.
Hang on, this isn't my coat.
Hang on, didn't you say you were away this week?
hang on to: typical: hang on to sth/sb. NOT for: letting go.
Hang on to the rope with both hands.
The child hung on to his mother's coat.
keep something and not give it away or sell it
typical: hang on to your money/an old book. NOT for: throwing something away.
You should hang on to your receipt.
She hung on to that old car for twenty years.
hang out: spend time somewhere or with friends in a relaxed way
typical: informal, hang out with friends/at the mall. NOT for: working or studying.
We usually hang out at Sam's place on weekends.
Who do you hang out with after school?
put wet clothes outside to dry
typical: hang out the washing, hang sth out. NOT for: using a dryer.
She hung out the washing before it started to rain.
I'll hang the sheets out in the garden.
hang up: typical: hang up (on sb), e.g. she hung up on me. NOT for: waiting on the line.
She hung up before I could explain.
put something on a hook or hanger
typical: hang sth up, hang up your coat. NOT for: throwing it on the floor.
Please hang up your coat in the hall.
He hung his jacket up behind the door.
have on: verb
be wearing something
typical: have sth on, e.g. she had a red coat on. NOT for: putting clothes on (use put on).
She had a long blue coat on.
What did he have on at the party?
verb
have a TV, radio, light or machine switched on and working
typical: have the TV/radio/heating on, have sth on. NOT for: wearing clothes.
She always has the radio on while she cooks.
Why do you have the heating on in July?
verb
have plans or an appointment
typical: have sth on, mostly in questions and negatives, BrE. NOT for: being busy at work in general.
Do you have anything on tonight?
I have nothing on this weekend.
verb
trick someone as a joke, BrE informal
typical: have sb on, often 'You're having me on!'. NOT for: telling a serious lie.
You're having me on! That can't be true.
Is he serious, or is he having us on?
head for: typical: head for home/the exit. NOT for: arriving there.
It's late, so I'm going to head for home.
We headed for the beach right after breakfast.
be moving toward a good or bad situation
typical: head for trouble/disaster/success. NOT for: places.
If you keep spending like this, you're heading for trouble.
The team is heading for the title.
head off: leave to go to a place
typical: head off to/for + place, informal. NOT for: coming back.
They headed off to the mountains on Friday.
I should head off; it's getting late.
stop something before it happens or gets worse
typical: head off a problem/an argument, head sth off. NOT for: causing it.
She spoke to him early to head off an argument.
We hope to head the strike off with new talks.
head out: leave a place and start a journey
typical: informal, head out (to + place). NOT for: arriving.
We head out at six tomorrow morning.
She headed out to the shops before the rain came.
hear about: be told news or facts about someone or something
typical: did you hear about ...? hear about sth. NOT for: knowing that something exists (use hear of).
Did you hear about the new teacher?
I only heard about the party yesterday.
hear from: get a message, call or letter from someone
typical: hear from sb, I hope to hear from you soon. NOT for: being told about someone by other people.
I haven't heard from her since June.
Have you heard from the company yet?
listen to someone speak at a meeting or event
typical: we'll hear from sb next. NOT for: getting letters.
Next we will hear from our guest speaker.
The committee heard from several local residents.
hence: shows that something is the result or the reason for what has just been said
typical: formal, often followed by a noun phrase, e.g. hence the delay. NOT for: casual speech; also not for time (ten days hence is old-fashioned).
Demand has doubled, hence the long queues outside the shop.
Our rent is low, hence we can afford better equipment.
Water expands when it freezes, hence the burst pipes in winter.
hit back: attack someone who has attacked you
typical: hit back (at sb). NOT for: starting a fight.
The boy hit back when the other kid pushed him.
The smaller team hit back with two quick goals.
answer criticism in a strong way
typical: hit back at critics. NOT for: agreeing with them.
The minister hit back at his critics on TV.
She hit back at the rumours with a public statement.
hit on: try to start a romantic relationship with someone, informal, mostly US
typical: hit on sb. NOT for: asking for help or directions.
A man was hitting on her at the bar.
He hit on my sister at the party.
find an idea or solution by chance or after thinking
typical: hit on an idea/a solution. NOT for: hitting something physically.
After weeks of trying, she hit on the right answer.
We hit on a plan that worked.
hit up: ask someone for money or a favour, informal, mostly US
typical: hit sb up for sth. NOT for: asking politely in a formal way.
He hit me up for twenty dollars again.
Don't hit your parents up for money every month.
contact someone, usually by phone or message, informal, mostly US
typical: hit me up, hit sb up later. NOT for: formal business messages.
Hit me up when you get to town.
I'll hit you up later about dinner.
hold against: blame someone or think less of them because of something they did
typical: hold sth against sb, e.g. I don't hold it against you. NOT for: forgiving.
I made a mistake, but please don't hold it against me.
She held his earlier lie against him for years.
hold back: stop someone or something from moving forward or developing
typical: hold sb/sth back, e.g. fear held him back. NOT for: helping progress.
Fear of failure is holding him back.
The bad weather held back the building work.
stop yourself from showing a feeling or doing something
typical: hold back tears/anger/a laugh. NOT for: showing feelings freely.
She couldn't hold back her tears.
He held back from saying what he really thought.
keep information or something for yourself
typical: hold back information/money. NOT for: sharing it.
The company held back some of the payment.
Don't hold back anything; tell me everything.
hold off: typical: hold off (on) sth, e.g. hold off on buying. NOT for: acting at once.
We decided to hold off on buying a new car.
Let's hold off until we hear from the bank.
not arrive or start, about rain or bad weather
typical: the rain held off. NOT for: starting to rain.
Luckily, the rain held off until the end of the match.
I hope the snow holds off until we get home.
keep an attacker or opponent away
typical: hold off an attack/a challenge. NOT for: giving up.
The defenders held off the attack for an hour.
She held off a late challenge to win the race.
hold on: verb
wait a moment, especially on the phone
typical: spoken, hold on a minute, hold on please. NOT for: ending a call.
Hold on, I'll see if she's in.
Can you hold on for a minute?
verb
grip something tightly
typical: hold on (to) sth, hold on tight. NOT for: letting go.
Hold on tight; the road is bumpy.
She held on to the railing.
verb
continue in a difficult situation
typical: hold on until help comes. NOT for: giving up.
The villagers held on until the rescue team arrived.
If we can hold on until spring, things will improve.
verb
keep something you already have and not lose it
typical: hold on to a job, a lead, a seat. NOT for: gripping with your hands.
He held on to his job through the crisis.
We held on to the lead until the final whistle.
hold on to: typical: hold on to sth/sb. NOT for: letting go.
Hold on to my hand when we cross the road.
He held on to the rope with both hands.
keep something and not give it up
typical: hold on to a lead/a job/a belief. NOT for: losing it.
The team held on to its lead until the end.
She held on to her dream of becoming a pilot.
hold out: verb
stretch out your hand or something in your hand
typical: hold out a hand/a cup, hold sth out. NOT for: keeping something back.
He held out his hand and smiled.
She held the letter out to me.
verb
say or believe that something good is possible
typical: hold out hope/the promise/the prospect of sth, often negative: not hold out much hope. NOT for: stretching out your hand.
Doctors don't hold out much hope of a full recovery.
The new treatment holds out the promise of fewer side effects.
verb
last or stay available for long enough
typical: supplies/food/money hold out. NOT for: running out.
The food will hold out for another week.
How long will the money hold out?
verb
refuse to give in to pressure or demands
typical: hold out for sth, hold out against sb. NOT for: surrendering.
The workers are holding out for better pay.
The town held out against the army for months.
hold over: delay something until a later time
typical: hold sth over, often a film or a decision. NOT for: finishing on time.
The decision was held over until next month.
The cinema held the film over for another week.
use something you know about someone to control them
typical: hold sth over sb. NOT for: forgiving a mistake.
Don't hold my mistake over me forever.
She always holds her past favours over me.
hold together: typical: an object holds together, e.g. the old bridge barely holds together. NOT for: coming apart.
The old bridge barely holds together.
This glue will hold the pieces together.
typical: a team/family/party holds together. NOT for: splitting up.
The family held together through hard times.
It's hard to hold a team together after so many losses.
hold up: verb
delay someone or something
typical: be held up, hold sb up, e.g. held up by traffic. NOT for: making something faster.
Sorry I'm late; I was held up in traffic.
Roadworks are holding up deliveries.
verb
rob a place or person using a weapon
typical: hold up a bank/shop; a hold-up. NOT for: stealing quietly.
Two men held up a bank in the city centre.
The shop was held up last night.
verb
support something so that it does not fall
typical: hold sth up, e.g. columns hold up the roof. NOT for: pulling something down.
Four stone columns hold up the roof.
He held the sign up above the crowd.
verb
stay strong or still be true when tested
typical: a story/an object holds up well. NOT for: breaking down.
His story didn't hold up when the police checked it.
The old tent held up well in the storm.
hook up: connect something to a power supply, network or other equipment
typical: hook sth up (to sth), hook up the printer. NOT for: disconnecting it.
Can you hook up the printer to my laptop?
He hooked the TV up to the internet.
meet or spend time with someone, informal
typical: hook up with sb; in US English sometimes romantic. NOT for: formal appointments.
Let's hook up after work for a coffee.
She hooked up with an old friend in Paris.
however: adds information that surprises or contrasts with what you have just said
typical: writing and formal speech, at the start of a sentence or between commas. NOT for: joining two clauses with only a comma (use 'but' or a full stop before 'however').
The hotel is beautiful. However, it is very far from the centre.
The film was long. I enjoyed it, however.
Many students passed. Some, however, will have to retake the exam.
hunt down: search until you find a person or thing
typical: hunt sb/sth down, e.g. hunt down a thief. NOT for: finding something by chance.
Police are trying to hunt down the thief.
I hunted down a copy of the book in a small shop.
hurry up: typical: Hurry up!, hurry sb up. NOT for: slowing down.
Hurry up, we'll miss the bus!
I tried to hurry him up, but he kept talking.
